title: Songhai Empire
capsule: The Songhai Empire was the largest state in West African history at its apex, centered on the great bend of the Niger River with its capital at Gao, and rose to dominance after Sunni Ali (r. 1464–1492) captured Timbuktu in 1468 and Djenne in 1473, displacing Mali as the paramount Sahelian power. Under Askia Muhammad I (r. 1493–1528) the empire organized a sophisticated provincial administration, standardized weights and measures, and made Timbuktu a leading center of Islamic scholarship. The empire began fragmenting under a succession of weaker rulers, and the Moroccan Sa'adian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur dispatched an army of Spanish and Portuguese renegades armed with firearms across the Sahara; this force destroyed the Songhai army at the Battle of Tondibi on 12 March 1591, sacked Gao and Timbuktu, and ended Songhai imperial authority.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territory along the Niger bend is attested by Arabic chronicles (al-Sadi's Tarikh al-Sudan, Ibn Battuta's predecessor accounts) and Moroccan campaign records; provincial boundaries in the Sahel and toward the forest zone are conjectural reconstructions with limited primary-source grounding.
